text: Imagine you're trying to quickly sign into your favorite music app and you accidentally type in the wrong password.
Should the application let you in because you were off by one letter or because your spelling was highly creative?
No. You expect it to follow a rigid rule.
Grant access only if the password is an exact match.
This demand for exactness is the foundation of traditional software.
A calculator executes mathematical operations exactly as instructed, without any interpretation.
A spreadsheet applies the formulas you enter to process your information, exactly the same way every single time.
This diagram maps out these rigid instructions.
A programmer writes the logic.
A user enters a password, hitting a checkpoint.
If it matches, the logic follows this path, opening the app.
Otherwise, it diverts to an error message.
Written rules return the same result every time.
But human communication rarely follows perfect logic.
Imagine trying to digitize a handwritten playlist for a homecoming dance,
covered in crossed-out song ideas and arrows pointing to replacements.
The notes are filled with vague abbreviations and inside jokes crammed into the margins, hiding the actual tracks you selected.
A programmer cannot write a separate instruction for every possible scribble, smudge, or pointing arrow on that page.
The rigid logic breaks down.
This is where artificial intelligence takes a different approach.
Instead of relying on pre-written instructions for every possible scenario,
a large language model, or LLM, identifies context.
An LLM learns patterns during training.
By recognizing how human language and notation generally work,
the system interprets your messy notes and generates a clean, usable list without explicit instructions for every mark.
AI is still software.
Humans still write the code that builds and trains these models.
The difference is they don't manually code a separate rule for every individual request.
We can look at a kitchen to see how these two distinct approaches operate in reality.
Look at this comparison.
Rule-based software operates like a cooking robot, executing a recipe.
Someone wrote down the exact steps.
The robot simply measures the ingredients, follows the instructions, and repeats the process.
It yields the exact same result every time.
By contrast, AI is like a chef who has learned by preparing hundreds of diverse dishes.
This chef recognizes deep relationships, which ingredients complement each other, and how heat changes flavor.
Because of this understanding, the chef doesn't need a recipe.
Operating on learned patterns, the chef recognizes pairings and substitutions without a recipe,
allowing for new, unexpected dishes.
Think about calculating your grade point average.
You input grades and credits into specific rows and columns.
That is structured data, information arranged into consistent, predefined fields.
Now imagine you snap a quick photo on a college campus to remember the name of a building.
That is unstructured data.
The visual information isn't stored into neat fields.
But AI can scan that unstructured visual data using context clues and partial signs to identify specific dorm buildings.
But relying on learned patterns introduces a critical downside.
AI responses are inherently harder to predict and inspect than a simple written password roll.
An AI might confidently name the wrong dorm building from your photo,
or misread an arrow on your handwritten playlist and accidentally skip your favorite song entirely.
It might look great, but still have mistakes.
Neither technology is universally superior.
We select them based on the demands of the task.
Different jobs need different tools.
Choose the tool that fits the work.
